# Probability of Returning to Zero Infinitely Often

## Setting Up the Problem

The standard formulation of this problem involves a **simple symmetric random walk** where $X_i$ are i.i.d. with:
$$P(X_i = 1) = P(X_i = -1) = \tfrac{1}{2}$$

and $S_0 = 0$. We seek $\mathbb{P}[S_n = 0 \text{ for infinitely many } n]$.

## Key Step 1: Recurrence of the Symmetric Random Walk

The walk $S_n$ is **recurrent** on $\mathbb{Z}$. A classic result (via the reflection principle or generating functions) shows that the probability of ever returning to 0, starting from 0, equals 1:

$$\mathbb{P}\left(\exists\, n \geq 1 : S_n = 0 \mid S_0 = 0\right) = 1$$

This is verified by noting the generating function of return probabilities $f_n = \mathbb{P}(T_1 = n)$ satisfies $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f_n = 1$, i.e., the return is certain.

## Key Step 2: The Strong Markov Property

Let $T_k$ denote the $k$-th return time to 0. By the **strong Markov property**, at each return time $T_k$, the process $\{S_{T_k + j} - S_{T_k}\}_{j \geq 0}$ is again a fresh copy of the random walk starting at 0. Therefore:

$$\mathbb{P}(T_{k+1} < \infty \mid T_k < \infty) = 1 \quad \text{for all } k \geq 1$$

## Key Step 3: Infinitely Many Returns

Chaining these together:

$$\mathbb{P}(T_1 < \infty,\, T_2 < \infty,\, \dots,\, T_k < \infty) = \prod_{j=1}^{k} \mathbb{P}(T_{j+1}<\infty \mid T_j<\infty) = 1^k = 1$$

Taking $k \to \infty$:

$$\mathbb{P}(S_n = 0 \text{ for infinitely many } n) = \lim_{k\to\infty} \mathbb{P}(T_1 < \infty, \dots, T_k < \infty) = 1$$

## Conclusion

The simple symmetric random walk is **recurrent**: it visits the origin (and indeed every integer) infinitely many times almost surely.

$$\boxed{1}$$
